entries.a5ffd42a6714dbdfd9ecb10b8fda726732a2a87d: <div sID="gen3547" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Deut.11" sID="Deut.11"/> <div eID="gen3547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3548" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3549" type="x-p"/> With this chapter Moses concludes his preface to the repetition of the statutes and judgments which they must observe to do. He repeats the general charge (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.1">ver. 1</reference>), and, having in the close of the foregoing chapter begun to mention the great things God had done among them, in this, I. He specifies several of the great works God had done before their eyes, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.2-Deut.11.7">ver. 2-7</reference>. II. He sets before them, for the future, life and death, the blessing and the curse, according as they did, or did not, keep God's commandments, that they should certainly prosper if they were obedient, should be blessed with plenty of all good things (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.8-Deut.11.15">ver. 8-15</reference>), and with victory over their enemies, and the enlargement of their coast thereby, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.22-Deut.11.25">ver. 22-25</reference>. But their disobedience would undoubtedly be their ruin, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.16-Deut.11.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>. III. He directs them what means to use that they might keep in mind the law of God, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.18-Deut.11.21">ver. 18-21</reference>. And, IV. Concludes all with solemnly charging them to choose which they would have, the blessing or the curse, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.26-Deut.11.32">ver. 26</reference>, &c.
entries.23462b4d1ccbf912c89d6a3086b7aa9cf84306cc: <div eID="gen3549" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3548" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Persuasives to Obedience. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3550" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Therefore thou shalt love the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, and keep his charge, and his statutes, and his judgments, and his commandments, alway. <hi type="super">2</hi> And know ye this day: for <hi type="italic">I speak</hi> not with your children which have not known, and which have not seen the chastisement of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, his greatness, his mighty hand, and his stretched out arm, <hi type="super">3</hi> And his miracles, and his acts, which he did in the midst of Egypt unto Pharaoh the king of Egypt, and unto all his land; <hi type="super">4</hi> And what he did unto the army of Egypt, unto their horses, and to their chariots; how he made the water of the Red sea to overflow them as they pursued after you, and <hi type="italic">how</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath destroyed them unto this day; <hi type="super">5</hi> And what he did unto you in the wilderness, until ye came into this place; <hi type="super">6</hi> And what he did unto Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, the son of Reuben: how the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up, and their households, and their tents, and all the substance that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in their possession, in the midst of all Israel: <hi type="super">7</hi> But your eyes have seen all the great acts of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> which he did. <div eID="gen3550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3551" type="x-p"/> Because <hi type="italic">God has made thee as the stars of heaven for multitude</hi> (so the preceding chapter concludes), <hi type="italic">therefore thou shalt love the Lord thy God</hi> (so this begins). Those whom God has built up into families, whose beginning was small, but whose latter end greatly increases, should use that as an argument with themselves why they should serve God. Thou shalt <hi type="italic">keep his charge,</hi> that is, the oracles of his word and ordinances of his worship, with which they were entrusted and for which they were accountable. It is a phrase often used concerning the office of the priests and Levites, for all Israel was a kingdom of priests, a holy nation. Observe the connection of these two: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt love the Lord</hi> and <hi type="italic">keep his charge,</hi> since love will work in obedience, and that only is acceptable obedience which flows from a principle of love. <reference osisRef="1John.5.3">1 John v. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen3551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3552" type="x-p"/> Mention is made of the great and terrible works of God which their <hi type="italic">eyes had seen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.11.7">v. 7</reference>. This part of his discourse Moses addresses to the <hi type="italic">seniors</hi> among the people, the elders in age; and probably the elders in office were so, and were now his immediate auditors: there were some among them that could remember their deliverance out of Egypt, all above fifty, and to them he speaks this, not to the children, who knew it by hearsay only, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.2">v. 2</reference>. Note, God's mercies to us when we were young we should remember and retain the impressions of when we are old; what our eyes have seen, especially in our early days, has affected us, and should be improved by us long after. They had seen what terrible judgments God had executed upon the enemies of Israel's peace, 1. Upon Pharaoh and the Egyptians that enslaved them. What a fine country was ruined and laid waste by one plague after another, to force Israel's enlargement! <reference osisRef="Deut.11.3">v. 3</reference>. What a fine army was entirely drowned in the Red Sea, to prevent Israel's being re-enslaved! <reference osisRef="Deut.11.4">v. 4</reference>. Thus did he give <hi type="italic">Egypt for their ransom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.43.3">Isa. xliii. 3</reference>. Rather shall that famous kingdom be destroyed than that Israel shall not be delivered. 2. Upon Dathan and Abiram that embroiled them. Remember <hi type="italic">what he did in the wilderness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.5">v. 5</reference>), by how many necessary <hi type="italic">chastisements</hi> (as they are called, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.2">v. 2</reference>) they were kept from ruining themselves, particularly when those daring Reubenites defied the authority of Moses and headed a dangerous rebellion against God himself, which threatened the ruin of a whole nation, and might have ended in that if the divine power had not immediately crushed the rebellion by burying the rebels alive, them and <hi type="italic">all that was in their possession,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.11.6">v. 6</reference>. What was done against them, though misinterpreted by the disaffected party (<reference osisRef="Num.16.41">Num. xvi. 41</reference>), was really done in mercy to Israel. To be saved from the mischiefs of insurrections at home is as great a kindness to a people, and therefore lays them under as strong obligations, as protection from the invasion of enemies abroad.
entries.ec5d08ad802ff6bae6a8d523ab77cd01ff5f646e: <div eID="gen3552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3553" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Therefore shall ye keep all the commandments which I command you this day, that ye may be strong, and go in and possess the land, whither ye go to possess it; <hi type="super">9</hi> And that ye may prolong <hi type="italic">your</hi> days in the land, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sware unto your fathers to give unto them and to their seed, a land that floweth with milk and honey. <hi type="super">10</hi> For the land, whither thou goest in to possess it, <hi type="italic">is</hi> not as the land of Egypt, from whence ye came out, where thou sowedst thy seed, and wateredst <hi type="italic">it</hi> with thy foot, as a garden of herbs: <hi type="super">11</hi> But the land, whither ye go to possess it, <hi type="italic">is</hi> a land of hills and valleys, <hi type="italic">and</hi> drinketh water of the rain of heaven: <hi type="super">12</hi> A land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God careth for: the eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God <hi type="italic">are</hi> always upon it, from the beginning of the year even unto the end of the year. 13 And it shall come to pass, if ye shall hearken diligently unto my commandments which I command you this day, to love the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul, <hi type="super">14</hi> That I will give <hi type="italic">you</hi> the rain of your land in his due season, the first rain and the latter rain, that thou mayest gather in thy corn, and thy wine, and thine oil. <hi type="super">15</hi> And I will send grass in thy fields for thy cattle, that thou mayest eat and be full. <hi type="super">16</hi> Take heed to yourselves, that your heart be not deceived, and ye turn aside, and serve other gods, and worship them; <hi type="super">17</hi> And <hi type="italic">then</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's wrath be kindled against you, and he shut up the heaven, that there be no rain, and that the land yield not her fruit; and <hi type="italic">lest</hi> ye perish quickly from off the good land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> giveth you. <div eID="gen3553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3554" type="x-p"/> Still Moses urges the same subject, as loth to conclude till he had gained his point. "<hi type="italic">If thou wilt enter into life,</hi> if thou wilt enter into Canaan, a type of that life, and find it a good land indeed to thee, <hi type="italic">keep the commandments: Keep all the commandments which I command you this day;</hi> love God, and serve him with all your heart." <div eID="gen3554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3555" type="x-p"/> I. Because this was the way to get and keep possession of the promised land. 1. It was the way to get possession (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">That you may be strong</hi> for war, and so <hi type="italic">go in and possess it.</hi> So little did they know either of hardship or hazard in the wars of Canaan that he does not say they should go in and fight for it; no, they had nothing in effect to do but go in and possess it. He does not go about to teach them the art of war, how to draw the bow, and use the sword, and keep ranks, that they might be strong, and go in and possess the land; no, but let them keep God's commandments, and their religion, while they are true to it, will be their strength, and secure their success. (2.) It was the way to keep possession (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">That you may prolong your days in this land</hi> that your eye is upon. Sin tends to the shortening of the days of particular persons and to the shortening of the days of a people's prosperity; but obedience will be a lengthening out of their tranquillity. <div eID="gen3555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3556" type="x-p"/> II. Because the land of Canaan, into which they were going, had a more sensible dependence upon the blessing of heaven than the land of Egypt had, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.10-Deut.11.12">v. 10-12</reference>. Egypt was a country fruitful enough, but it was all flat, and was watered, not as other countries with rain (it is said of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.18">Zech. xiv. 18</reference>, that it <hi type="italic">has no rain</hi>), but by the overflowing of the river Nile at a certain season of the year, to the improving of which there was necessary a great deal of the art and labour of the husbandman, so that in Egypt a man must bestow as much cost and pains upon a field as upon a garden of herbs. And this made them the more apt to imagine that the power of their own hands got them this wealth. But the land of Canaan was an uneven country, a land of hills and valleys, which not only gave a more pleasing prospect to the eye, but yielded a greater variety of soils for the several purposes of the husbandman. It was a land that had no great rivers in it, except Jordan, but <hi type="italic">drank water of the rain of heaven,</hi> and so, 1. Saved them a great deal of labour. While the Egyptians were ditching and guttering in the fields, up to the knees in mud, to bring water to their land, which otherwise would soon become like the heath in the wilderness, the Israelites could sit in their houses, warm and easy, and leave it to God to water their land with the former and the latter rain, which is called <hi type="italic">the river of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.65.9">Ps. lxv. 9</reference>), perhaps in allusion to, and contempt of, the river of Egypt, which that nation was so proud of. Note, The better God has provided, by our outward condition, for our ease and convenience, the more we should abound in his service: the less we have to do for our bodies the more we should do for God and our souls. 2. So he directed them to look upwards to God, who <hi type="italic">giveth us rain from heaven and fruitful seasons</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.17">Acts xiv. 17</reference>), and promised to be himself as <hi type="italic">the dew unto Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.14.5">Hos. xiv. 5</reference>. Note, (1.) Mercies bring with them the greatest comfort and sweetness when we see them coming from heaven, the immediate gifts of divine Providence. (2.) The closer dependence we have upon God the more cheerful we should be in our obedience to him. See how Moses here magnifies the land of Canaan above all other lands, that the <hi type="italic">eyes of God were always upon it,</hi> that is, they should be so, to see that nothing was wanting, while they kept close to God and duty; its fruitfulness should be not so much the happy effect of its soil as the immediate fruit of the divine blessing; this may be inferred from its present state, for it is said to be at this day, now that God has departed from it, as barren a spot of ground as perhaps any under heaven. Call it not <hi type="italic">Naomi:</hi> call it <hi type="italic">Marah.</hi> <div eID="gen3556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3557" type="x-p"/> III. Because God would certainly bless them with an abundance of all good things if they would love him and serve him (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.13-Deut.11.15">v. 13-15</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will give you the rain of your land in due season,</hi> so that they should neither want it when the ground called for it nor have it in excess; but they should have the former rain, which fell at seed-time, and the latter rain, which fell before the harvest, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.7">Amos iv. 7</reference>. This represented all the seasonable blessings which God would bestow upon them, especially spiritual comforts, which should come <hi type="italic">as the latter and former, rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.6.3">Hos. vi. 3</reference>. And the earth thus watered produced, 1. Fruits for the service of man, <hi type="italic">corn and wine, and oil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.13-Ps.104.15">Ps. civ. 13-15</reference>. 2. Grass for the cattle, that they also might be serviceable to man, that <hi type="italic">he might eat of them and be full,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.11.15">v. 15</reference>. Godliness hath here the <hi type="italic">promise of the life that now is;</hi> but the favour of God shall put gladness into the heart, more than the increase of corn, and wine, and oil will. <div eID="gen3557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3558" type="x-p"/> IV. Because their revolt from God to idols. would certainly be their ruin: <hi type="italic">Take heed that your hearts be not deceived,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.11.16-Deut.11.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. All that forsake God to set their affection upon, or pay their devotion to, any creature, will find themselves wretchedly deceived to their own destruction; and this will aggravate it that it was purely for want of taking heed. A little care would have prevented their being imposed upon by the great deceiver. To awaken them to take heed, Moses here tells them plainly that if they should <hi type="italic">turn aside to other gods,</hi> 1. They would provoke the wrath of God against them; and <hi type="italic">who knows the power of that anger?</hi> 2. Good things would be turned away from them; the heaven would withhold its rain, and then of course the earth would not yield its fruit. 3. Evil things would come upon them; they would perish quickly from off this good land. And the better the land was the more grievous it would be to perish from it. The goodness of the land would not be their security, when the badness of the inhabitants had made them ripe for ruin.
entries.db146caf99e2079bd2bddc421c92d5a163e86608: <div eID="gen3558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3559" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Therefore shall ye lay up these my words in your heart and in your soul, and bind them for a sign upon your hand, that they may be as frontlets between your eyes. <hi type="super">19</hi> And ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, when thou liest down, and when thou risest up. <hi type="super">20</hi> And thou shalt write them upon the door posts of thine house, and upon thy gates: <hi type="super">21</hi> That your days may be multiplied, and the days of your children, in the land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sware unto your fathers to give them, as the days of heaven upon the earth. <hi type="super">22</hi> For if ye shall diligently keep all these commandments which I command you, to do them, to love the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, to walk in all his ways, and to cleave unto him; <hi type="super">23</hi> Then will the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> drive out all these nations from before you, and ye shall possess greater nations and mightier than yourselves. <hi type="super">24</hi> Every place whereon the soles of your feet shall tread shall be yours: from the wilderness and Lebanon, from the river, the river Euphrates, even unto the uttermost sea shall your coast be. <hi type="super">25</hi> There shall no man be able to stand before you: <hi type="italic">for</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God shall lay the fear of you and the dread of you upon all the land that ye shall tread upon, as he hath said unto you. <div eID="gen3559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3560" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Moses repeats the directions he had given for the guidance and assistance of the people in their obedience, and for the keeping up of religion among them (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.18-Deut.11.20">v. 18-20</reference>), which is much to the same purport with what we had before, <reference osisRef="Deut.6.6">ch. vi. 6</reference>, &c. Let us all be directed by the three rules here given:—1. Let our hearts be filled with the word of God: <hi type="italic">Lay up these words in your heart and in your soul.</hi> The heart must be the treasury or store-house in which the word of God must be laid up, to be used upon all occasions. We cannot expect good practices in the conversation, unless there be good thoughts, good affections, and good principles, in the heart. 2. Let our eyes be fixed upon the word of God. "Bind these words for a sign <hi type="italic">upon your hand,</hi> which is always in view (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.16">Isa. xlix. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">and as frontlets between your eyes,</hi> which you cannot avoid the sight of; let them be as ready and familiar to you, and have your eye as constantly upon them, as if they were <hi type="italic">written upon your door-posts,</hi> and could not be overlooked either when you go out or when you come in." Thus we must <hi type="italic">lay God's judgments before us,</hi> having a constant regard to them, as the guide of our way, as the rule of our work, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.30">Ps. cxix. 30</reference>. 3. Let our tongues be employed about the word of God. Let it be the subject of our familiar discourse, wherever we are; especially with our children, who must be taught the service of God, as the one thing needful, much more needful than either the rules of decency or the calling they must live by in this world. Great care and pains must be taken to acquaint children betimes, and to affect them, with the word of God and the wondrous things of his law. Nor will any thing contribute more to the prosperity and perpetuity of religion in a nation than the good education of children: if the seed be holy, it is the substance of a land. <div eID="gen3560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3561" type="x-p"/> II. He repeats the assurances he had before given them, in God's name, of prosperity and success if they were obedient. 1. They should have a happy settlement, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.21">v. 21</reference>. Their days should be multiplied; and, when they were fulfilled, the days of their children likewise should be many, as the days of heaven, that is, Canaan should be sure to them and their heirs for ever, as long as the world stands, if they did not by their own sin throw themselves out of it. 2. It should not be in the power of their enemies to give them any disturbance, nor make them upon any account uneasy. "If you will <hi type="italic">keep God's commandments,</hi> and be careful to do your duty (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.22">v. 22</reference>), God will not only crown the labours of the husbandman with plenty of the fruits of the earth, but he will own and succeed the more glorious undertakings of the men of war. Victory shall attend your arms; which way soever they turn, God will drive out these nations, and put you in possession of their land," <reference osisRef="Deut.11.23-Deut.11.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. Their territories should be enlarged to the utmost extent of the promise, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Gen. xv. 18</reference>. And all their neighbours should stand in awe of them, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.25">v. 25</reference>. Nothing contributes more to the making of a nation considerable abroad, valuable to its friends and formidable to its enemies, than religion reigning in it; for who can be against those that have God for them? And he is certainly for those that are sincerely for him, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.34">Prov. xiv. 34</reference>.
entries.6270c9597974ab4cd0ba7c63e44c8d47083622b6: <div eID="gen3561" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Blessing and the Curse. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3562" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse; <hi type="super">27</hi> A blessing, if ye obey the commandments of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, which I command you this day: <hi type="super">28</hi> And a curse, if ye will not obey the commandments of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, but turn aside out of the way which I command you this day, to go after other gods, which ye have not known. <hi type="super">29</hi> And it shall come to pass, when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hath brought thee in unto the land whither thou goest to possess it, that thou shalt put the blessing upon mount Gerizim, and the curse upon mount Ebal. <hi type="super">30</hi> <hi type="italic">Are</hi> they not on the other side Jordan, by the way where the sun goeth down, in the land of the Canaanites, which dwell in the champaign over against Gilgal, beside the plains of Moreh? <hi type="super">31</hi> For ye shall pass over Jordan to go in to possess the land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God giveth you, and ye shall possess it, and dwell therein. <hi type="super">32</hi> And ye shall observe to do all the statutes and judgments which I set before you this day. <div eID="gen3562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3563" type="x-p"/> Here Moses concludes his general exhortations to obedience; and his management is very affecting, and such as, one would think, should have engaged them for ever to God, and should have left impressions upon them never to be worn out. <div eID="gen3563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3564" type="x-p"/> I. He sums up all his arguments for obedience in two words, <hi type="italic">the blessing and the curse</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.26">v. 26</reference>), that is, the rewards and the punishments, as they stand in the promises and the threatenings, which are the great sanctions of the law, taking hold of hope and fear, those two handles of the soul, by which it is caught, held, and managed. These two, the blessing and the curse, he set before them, that is, 1. He explained them, that they might know them; he enumerated the particulars contained both in the blessing and in the curse, that they might see the more fully how desirable the blessing was, and how dreadful the curse. 2. He confirmed them, that they might believe them, made it evident to them, by the proofs he produced of his own commission, that the blessing was not a fool's paradise, nor the curse a bugbear, but that both were real declarations of the purpose of God concerning them. 3. He charged them to choose which of these they would have, so fairly does he deal with them, and so far is he from <hi type="italic">putting out the eyes of these men,</hi> as he was charged, <reference osisRef="Num.16.14">Num. xvi. 14</reference>. They and we are plainly told on what terms we stand with Almighty God. (1.) If we be obedient to his laws, we may be sure of a blessing, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.27">v. 27</reference>. But, (2.) If we be disobedient, we may be as sure of a curse, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.28">v. 28</reference>. <hi type="italic">Say you to the righteous</hi> (for God has said it, and all the world cannot unsay it) that <hi type="italic">it shall be well with them: but woe to the wicked, it shall be ill with them.</hi> <div eID="gen3564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3565" type="x-p"/> II. He appoints a public and solemn proclamation to be made of the blessing and curse which he had set before them, upon the two mountains of Gerizim and Ebal, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.29-Deut.11.30">v. 29, 30</reference>. We have more particular directions for this solemnity in <reference osisRef="Deut.27.11">ch. xxvii. 11</reference>, &c., and an account of the performance of it, <reference osisRef="John.8.33">Josh. viii. 33</reference>, &c. It was to be done, and was done, immediately upon their coming into Canaan, that when they first took possession of that land they might know upon what terms they stood. The place where this was to be done is particularly described by Moses, though he never saw it, which is one circumstance among many that evidences his divine instructions. It is said be near the <hi type="italic">plain,</hi> or <hi type="italic">oaks,</hi> or <hi type="italic">meadows,</hi> of <hi type="italic">Moreh,</hi> which was one of the first places that Abraham came to in Canaan; so that in sending them thither, to hear the blessing and the curse, God reminded them of the promise he made to Abraham in that very place, <reference osisRef="Gen.12.6-Gen.12.7">Gen. xii. 6, 7</reference>. The mention of this appointment here serves, 1. For the encouragement of their faith in the promise of God, that they should be masters of Canaan quickly. Do it (says Moses) on the other side Jordan (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.30">v. 30</reference>), for you may be confident <hi type="italic">you shall pass over Jordan,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.11.31">v. 31</reference>. The institution of this service to be done in Canaan was an assurance to them that they should be brought into possession of it, and a token like that which God gave to Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.12">Exod. iii. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">You shall serve God upon this mountain.</hi> And, 2. It serves for an engagement upon them to be obedient, that they might escape that curse, and obtain that blessing, which, besides what they had already heard, they must shortly be witnesses to the solemn publication of (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.32">v. 32</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You shall observe to do the statutes and judgements,</hi> that you may not in that solemnity be witnesses against yourselves."  <chapter eID="Deut.11"/> <div eID="gen3565" type="x-p"/>

entries.b467181e9d2573b33842179aef7647ec464f568f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1743"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.11.1-Deut.11.32">De 11:1-32</reference>. An Exhortation to Obedience.</title> <div sID="gen2329" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1743"/><hi type="bold">1. Therefore thou shalt love the Lord thy God, and keep his charge--</hi>The reason for the frequent repetition of the same or similar counsels is to be traced to the infantine character and state of the church, which required line upon line and precept upon precept. Besides, the Israelites were a headstrong and perverse people, impatient of control, prone to rebellion, and, from their long stay in Egypt, so violently addicted to idolatry, that they ran imminent risk of being seduced by the religion of the country to which they were going, which, in its characteristic features, bore a strong resemblance to that of the country they had left. <div eID="gen2329" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe4337a131a2ea5264120a2501ef5ef7f5d1eea2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1744"/><div sID="gen2330" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1744"/><hi type="bold">2-9. I speak not with your children which have not known ... But your eyes have seen all the great acts of the Lord which he did--</hi>Moses is here giving a brief summary of the marvels and miracles of awful judgment which God had wrought in effecting their release from the tyranny of Pharaoh, as well as those which had taken place in the wilderness. He knew that he might dwell upon these, for he was addressing many who had been witnesses of those appalling incidents. For it will be remembered that the divine threatening that they should die in the wilderness, and its execution, extended only to males from twenty years and upward, who were able to go forth to war. No males under twenty years of age, no females, and none of the tribe of Levi, were objects of the denunciation (see Nu 14:28-30; 16:49). There might, therefore, have been many thousands of the Israelites at that time of whom Moses could say, "Your eyes have seen all the great acts which He did"; and with regard to those the historic review of Moses was well calculated to stir up their minds to the duty and advantages of obedience. <div eID="gen2330" type="x-p"/>
entries.1af5376c9ea87e393d3b213e8a3aa89b9ef3712a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1745"/><div sID="gen2331" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1745"/><hi type="bold">10-12. For the land, whither thou goest in to possess it, is not as the land of Egypt, from whence ye came out--</hi>The physical features of Palestine present a striking contrast to those of the land of bondage. A widely extending plain forms the cultivated portion of Egypt, and on the greater part of this low and level country rain never falls. This natural want is supplied by the annual overflow of the Nile, and by artificial means from the same source when the river has receded within its customary channel. Close by the bank the process of irrigation is very simple. The cultivator opens a small sluice on the edge of the square bed in which seed has been sown, making drill after drill; and when a sufficient quantity of water has poured in, he shuts it up with his foot. Where the bank is high, the water is drawn up by hydraulic engines, of which there are three kinds used, of different power, according to the subsidence of the stream. The water is distributed in small channels or earthen conduits, simple in construction, worked by the foot, and formed with a mattock by the gardener who directs their course, and which are banked up or opened, as occasion may require, by pressing in the soil with the foot. Thus was the land watered in which the Israelites had dwelt so long. Such vigilance and laborious industry would not be needed in the promised land. Instead of being visited with moisture only at one brief season and left during the rest of the year under a withering blight, every season it would enjoy the benign influences of a genial climate. The hills would attract the frequent clouds, and in the refreshing showers the blessing of God would especially rest upon the land. <div eID="gen2331" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee77f7105448e46f7e8d040383ada8d6c712c332: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1747"/><div sID="gen2333" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1747"/><hi type="bold">14. the first rain and the latter rain--</hi>The early rain commenced in autumn, that is, chiefly during the months of September and October, while the latter rain fell in the spring of the year, that is, during the months of March and April. It is true that occasional showers fell all the winter; but, at the autumnal and vernal seasons, they were more frequent, copious, and important; for the early rain was necessary, after a hot and protracted summer, to prepare the soil for receiving the seed; and the latter rain, which shortly preceded the harvest, was of the greatest use in invigorating the languishing powers of vegetation (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.24">Jr 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.23">Joe 2:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.7">Am 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.7">Jas 5:7</reference>). <div eID="gen2333" type="x-p"/>
entries.99017198ab2c54ad2d17127847f977baeac11f0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1748"/><div sID="gen2334" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1748"/><hi type="bold">15-17. I will send grass in thy fields for thy cattle--</hi>Undoubtedly the special blessing of the former and the latter rain [De 11:14] was one principal cause of the extraordinary fertility of Canaan in ancient times. That blessing was promised to the Israelites as a temporal reward for their fidelity to the national covenant [De 11:13]. It was threatened to be withdrawn on their disobedience or apostasy; and most signally is the execution of that threatening seen in the present sterility of Palestine. MR. LowthIAN, an English farmer, who was struck during his journey from Joppa to Jerusalem by not seeing a blade of grass, where even in the poorest localities of Britain some wild vegetation is found, directed his attention particularly to the subject, and pursued the inquiry during a month's residence in Jerusalem, where he learned that a miserably small quantity of milk is daily sold to the inhabitants at a dear rate, and that chiefly asses' milk. "Most clearly," says he, "did I perceive that the barrenness of large portions of the country was owing to the cessation of the early and latter rain, and that the absence of grass and flowers made it no longer the land (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.9">De 11:9</reference>) flowing with milk and honey." <div eID="gen2334" type="x-p"/>
entries.84855a3e9f6efbcd582e080a8791f933923e4c35: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1749"/><div sID="gen2335" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1749"/><hi type="bold">18-25. lay up these my words in your heart and in your soul, and bind them--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Deut.6.1">De 6:1</reference>). <div eID="gen2335" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b0f797f8567c7ce5ec7fa35fdabb6c07a9a2555: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1751"/><div sID="gen2341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1751"/><hi type="bold">26-32. Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Deut.27.11">De 27:11</reference>). <chapter eID="Deut.11"/>

entries.a6f71f185c7b059227c5f48f0407217dcd7662e7: <div eID="gen6668" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen6669" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6670" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6670" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6669" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6671" type="x-p"/> The people are exhorted to obedience from a consideration of God's goodness to their fathers in Egypt, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.1-Deu.11.4">Deu 11:1-4</reference>, and what he did in the wilderness, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.5">Deu 11:5</reference>, and the judgment on Dathan and Abiram, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.6">Deu 11:6</reference>, and from the mercies of God in general, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.7-Deu.11.9">Deu 11:7-9</reference>. A comparative description of Egypt and Canaan, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.10-Deu.11.12">Deu 11:10-12</reference>. Promises to obedience, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.13-Deu.11.15">Deu 11:13-15</reference>. Dissuasives from idolatry, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.16">Deu 11:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.17">Deu 11:17</reference>. The words of God to be laid up in their hearts, to be for a sign on their hands, foreheads, gates, etc., <reference osisRef="Deu.11.18">Deu 11:18</reference>, taught to their children, made the subject of frequent conversation, to the end that their days may be multiplied, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.19-Deu.11.21">Deu 11:19-21</reference>. If obedient, God shall give them possession of the whole land, and not one of their enemies shall be able to withstand them, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.22-Deu.11.25">Deu 11:22-25</reference>. Life and death, a blessing and a curse, are set before them, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.26-Deu.11.28">Deu 11:26-28</reference>. The blessings to be put on Mount Gerizim and the curses on Mount Ebal, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.29">Deu 11:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.30">Deu 11:30</reference>. The promise that they should pass over Jordan, and observe these statutes in the promised land, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.31">Deu 11:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.32">Deu 11:32</reference>. <div eID="gen6671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6672" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen6672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6673" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt love the Lord - Because without this there could be no obedience to the Divine testimonies, and no happiness in the soul; for the heart that is destitute of the love of God, is empty of all good, and consequently miserable. See the note on <reference osisRef="Deu.10.12">Deu 10:12</reference>.
entries.1ab04bd0c62453a3841e4abf404b451699bce230: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen6673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6674" type="x-p"/> What he did unto Dathan, etc. - See the notes on Numbers 16 (note).
entries.fcef642c460e6469a85cee0578a7d9c36343f8f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen6674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6675" type="x-p"/> Therefore shall ye keep all the commandments - Because God can execute such terrible judgments, and because he has given such proofs of his power and justice; and because, in similar provocations, he may be expected to act in a similar way; therefore keep his charge, that he may keep you unto everlasting life.
entries.6637a0d64b31d8ce3f960ec23fea4db96259bdab: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen6675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6676" type="x-p"/> Wateredst it with thy foot - Rain scarcely ever falls in Egypt, and God supplies the lack of it by the inundations of the Nile. In order to water the grounds where the inundations do not extend, water is collected in ponds, and directed in streamlets to different parts of the field where irrigation is necessary. It is no unusual thing in the East to see a man, with a small mattock, making a little trench for the water to run by, and as he opens the passage, the water following, he uses his foot to raise up the mould against the side of this little channel, to prevent the water from being shed unnecessarily before it reaches the place of its destination. Thus he may be said to water the ground with his foot. See several useful observations on this subject in Mr. Harmer, vol. i., pp. 23-26, and vol. iii., p. 141. "For watering land an instrument called janta is often used in the north of Bengal: It consists of a wooden trough, about fifteen feet long, six inches wide, and ten inches deep, which is placed on a horizontal beam lying on bamboos fixed in the bank of a pond or river in the form of a gallows. One end of the trough rests upon the bank, where a gutter is prepared to carry off the water, and the other is dipped into the water by a man standing on a stage near that end, and plunging it in with his foot. A long bamboo, with a large weight of earth at the farther end of it, is fastened to that end of the janta near the river, and passing over the gallows, poises up the janta full of water, and causes it to empty itself into the gutter." This, Mr. Ward supposes, illustrates this passage. See Hindoo Customs, etc., vol. iii., p. 104. But after all, the expression, wateredst it with thy foot, may mean no more than doing it by labor; for, as in the land of Egypt there is scarcely any rain, the watering of gardens, etc., must have been all artificial. But in Judea it was different, as there they had their proper seasons of rain. The compound word ברגל beregel, with, under, or by the foot, is used to signify any thing under the power, authority, etc., of a person; and this very meaning it has in the sixth verse, all the substance that was in their possession, is, literally, all the substance that was under their feet, ברגליהם beragleyhem, that is, in their power, possession, or what they had acquired by their labor.
entries.4551f67f7a7b0ee823d90f9b09ba2ff533a475a6: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen6676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6677" type="x-p"/> The rain - in his due season, the first rain and the latter rain - By the first or former rain we are to understand that which fell in Judea about November, when they sowed their seed, and this served to moisten and prepare the ground for the vegetation of the seed. The latter rain fell about April, when the corn was well grown up, and served to fill the ears, and render them plump and perfect. Rain rarely fell in Judea at any other seasons than these. If the former rain were withheld, or not sent in due season, there could be no vegetation: if the latter rain were withheld, or not sent in its due season, there could be no full corn in the ear, and consequently no harvest. Of what consequence then was it that they should have their rain in due season! God, by promising this provided they were obedient, and threatening to withhold it should they be disobedient, shows that it is not a general providence that directs these things, but that the very rain of heaven falls by particular direction, and the showers are often regulated by an especial providence.
entries.59b3204887ff4a157d447bf75a0d5b36c5f6d9cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen6677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6678" type="x-p"/> Therefore shall ye lay up these my words - See <reference osisRef="Deu.6.4-Deu.6.8">Deu 6:4-8</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Exo.13.9">Exo 13:9</reference> (note).
entries.a57674cb4ebb7f42c77f0f68834bcb96555b3645: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen6678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6679" type="x-p"/> From the river - Euphrates, which was on the east, to the uttermost sea - the Mediterranean, which lay westward of the promised land. This promise, notwithstanding the many provocations of the Israelites, was fulfilled in the time of Solomon, for "he reigned over all the kings from the river (Euphrates) even unto the land of the Philistines, and to the border of Egypt." See <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.26">2Chr 9:26</reference>, and the note, <reference osisRef="Num.34.12">Num 34:12</reference> (note).
entries.e20d3fb5ecfdbeab7187bbbe45e2fb7e90d5bb74: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen6679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6680" type="x-p"/> Behold, I set before you - a blessing and a curse - If God had not put it in the power of this people either to obey or disobey; if they had not had a free will, over which they had complete authority, to use it either in the way of willing or nilling; could God, with any propriety, have given such precepts as these, sanctioned with such promises and threatenings? If they were not free agents, they could not be punished for disobedience, nor could they, in any sense of the word, have been rewardable for obedience. A Stone is not rewardable because, in obedience to the laws of gravitation, it always tends to the center; nor is it punishable be cause, in being removed from that center, in its tending or falling towards it again it takes away the life of a man. <div eID="gen6680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6681" type="x-p"/> That God has given man a free, self-determining Will, which cannot be forced by any power but that which is omnipotent, and which God himself never will force, is declared in the most formal manner through the whole of the sacred writings. No argument can affect this, while the Bible is considered as a Divine revelation; no sophistry can explain away its evidence, as long as the accountableness of man for his conduct is admitted, and as long as the eternal bounds of moral good and evil remain, and the essential distinctions between vice and virtue exist. If ye will obey, (for God is ever ready to assist), ye shall live; if ye will disobey and refuse that help, ye shall die. So hath Jehovah spoken, and man cannot reverse it.
entries.e8b01ad80a57a0d3506ebeb23435a5c8129dccef: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen6681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6682" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt put the blessing upon Mount Gerizim, and the curse upon Mount Ebal - The etymology of these names may be supposed to cast some light on this institution. גרזים gerizzim, from גרז garaz, to cut, cut off, cut down; hence גרזים gerizzim, the cutters down, fellers, and reapers or harvest-men, this mountain being supposed to have its name from its great fertility, or the abundance of the crops it yielded, which is a possible case. Of עיבל ebal or eybal the root is not found in Hebrew; but in Arabic abala signifies rough, rugged, curled, etc.; and abalo, from the same root, signifies white stones, and a mountain in which such stones are found; alabalo, the mount of white stones. See Giggeius and Golius. And as it is supposed that the mountain had this name because of its barrenness, on this metaphorical interpretation the sense of the passage would appear to be the following: God will so superintend the land, and have it continually under the eye of his watchful providence, that no change can happen in it but according to his Divine counsel, so that its fertility shall ever be the consequence of the faithful obedience of its inhabitants, and a proof of the blessing of God upon it; on the contrary, its barrenness shall be a proof that the people have departed from their God, and that his curse has in consequence fallen upon the land. See the manner of placing these blessings and curses, <reference osisRef="Deu.27.12">Deu 27:12</reference>, etc. That Gerizim is very fruitful, and that Ebal is very barren, is the united testimony of all who have traveled in those parts. See Ludolf, Reland, Rab, Benjamin, and Mr. Maundrell. Sychem lies in the valley between these two mountains. <div eID="gen6682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6683" type="x-p"/> That the land of Judea was naturally very fertile, can scarcely be supposed by any who considers the accounts given of it by travelers; with the exception of a few districts, the whole land is dry, stony, and barren, and particularly all the southern parts of Judea, and all the environs of Jerusalem, most of which are represented as absolutely incapable of cultivation. How then could it ever support its vast number of inhabitants? By the especial providence of God. While God kept that people under his continual protection, their land was a paradise; they lent to all nations and borrowed from none. What has it been since? A demi-solitude, because that especial blessing no longer descends upon it. No land, says Calmet, was more fertile while under the benediction of God; none more barren when under his curse. Its present state is a proof of the declaration of Moses, <reference osisRef="Deu.28.23">Deu 28:23</reference> : "The heaven over their head is brass; the earth under their feet, iron." The land itself, in its present state is an ample proof of the authenticity of the Pentateuch. Should facts of this kind be lost sight of by any who read the sacred writings?  <chapter eID="Deut.11"/> <div eID="gen6683" type="x-p"/>

entries.43bd97c01d1556902f6b93d2c1baf2f8c230df87: In <reference osisRef="Deut.11.1-Deut.11.12">Deu 11:1-12</reference> the other feature in the divine requirements (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.12">Deu 10:12</reference>), viz., love to the Lord their God, is still more fully developed. Love was to show itself in the distinct perception of what had to be observed towards Jehovah (to “<hi type="italic">keep His charge</hi>,” see at <reference osisRef="Lev.8.35">Lev 8:35</reference>), i.e., in the perpetual observance of His commandments and rights. The words, “<hi type="italic">and His statutes</hi>,” etc., serve to explain the general notion, “His charge.” “<hi type="italic">All days</hi>,” as in Deu 4:10. <div eID="gen2273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2274" type="x-p"/> To awaken this love they were now to know, i.e., to ponder and lay to heart, the discipline of the Lord their God. The words from “<hi type="italic">for</hi> (I speak) <hi type="italic">not</hi>” to “<hi type="italic">have not seen</hi>” are a parenthetical clause, by which Moses would impress his words most strongly upon the hearts of the older generation, which had witnessed the acts of the Lord. The clause is without any verb or predicate, but this can easily be supplied from the sense. The best suggestion is that of <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>, viz., ההוּא הדּבר, “for it is not with your children that I have to do,” not to them that this admonition applies. Moses refers to the children who had been born in the desert, as distinguished from those who, though not twenty years old when the Israelites came out of Egypt, had nevertheless seen with their own eyes the plagues inflicted upon Egypt, and who were now of mature age, viz., between forty and sixty years old, and formed, as the older and more experienced generation, the stock and kernel of the congregation assembled round him now. To the words, “<hi type="italic">which have not known and have not seen</hi>,” it is easy to supply from the context, “what ye have known and seen.” The accusatives from “the chastisement” onwards belong to the verb of the principal sentence, “know ye this day.” The accusatives which follow show what we are to understand by “the chastisement of the Lord,” viz., the mighty acts of the Lord to Egypt and to Israel in the desert. The object of them all was to <hi type="italic">educate</hi> Israel in the fear and love of God. In this sense Moses calls them מוּסר (<hi type="italic">Eng. Ver. chastisement</hi>), παιδεία, i.e., not punishment only, but education by the manifestation of love as well as punishment (like יסּר in <reference osisRef="Deut.4.36">Deu 4:36</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.1.2">Pro 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.8">Pro 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.4.1">Pro 4:1</reference>, etc.). “<hi type="italic">His greatness</hi>,” etc., as in <reference osisRef="Deut.3.24">Deu 3:24</reference> and Deu 4:34. On the signs and acts in Egypt, see at <reference osisRef="Deut.4.34">Deu 4:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.6.22">Deu 6:22</reference>; and on those at the Red Sea, at Ex 14. פּניהם - הצּיף אשׁר, “<hi type="italic">over whose face He made the waters of the Red Sea to flow;</hi>” cf. Exo 14:26. - By the acts of God in the desert (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.5">Deu 11:5</reference>) we are not to understand the chastenings in Num 11-15 either solely or pre-eminently, but all the manifestations of the omnipotence of God in the guidance of Israel, proofs of love as well as the penal wonders. Of the latter, the miraculous destruction of the company of Korah is specially mentioned in <reference osisRef="Deut.11.6">Deu 11:6</reference> (cf. Num 16:31-33). Here Moses only mentions Dathan and Abiram, the followers of Korah, and not Korah himself, probably from regard to his sons, who were not swallowed up by the earth along with their father, but had lived to perpetuate the family of Korah. “<hi type="italic">Everything existing, which was in their following</hi>” (see <reference osisRef="Exod.11.8">Exo 11:8</reference>), does not mean their possessions, but their servants, and corresponds to “all the men who belonged to Korah” in Num 16:32, whereas the possessions mentioned there are included here in the “tents.” היקוּם is only applied to living beings, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.7.4">Gen 7:4</reference> and Gen 7:23. - In <reference osisRef="Deut.11.7">Deu 11:7</reference> the reason is given for the admonition in <reference osisRef="Deut.11.2">Deu 11:2</reference> : the elders were to know (discern) the educational purpose of God in those mighty acts of the Lord, because they had seen them with their own eyes. <div eID="gen2274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2275" type="x-p"/> And this knowledge was to impel them to keep the law, that they might be strong, i.e., spiritually strong (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.38">Deu 1:38</reference>), and not only go into the promised land, but also live long therein (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.4.26">Deu 4:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.6.3">Deu 6:3</reference>). - In <reference osisRef="Deut.11.10-Deut.11.12">Deu 11:10-12</reference> Moses adduces a fresh motive for his admonition to keep the law with fidelity, founded upon the peculiar nature of the land. Canaan was a land the fertility of which was not dependent, like that of Egypt, upon its being watered by the hand of man, but was kept up by the rain of heaven which was sent down by God the Lord, so that it depended entirely upon the Lord how long its inhabitants should live therein. Egypt is described by Moses as a land which Israel sowed with seed, and watered with its foot like a garden of herbs. In Egypt there is hardly any rain at all (cf. <hi type="italic">Herod</hi>. ii. 4, <hi type="italic">Diod. Sic.</hi> i. 41, and other evidence in Hengstenberg’s <hi type="italic">Egypt and the Books of Moses</hi>, pp. 217ff.). The watering of the land, which produces its fertility, is dependent upon the annual overflowing of the Nile, and, as this only lasts for about 100 days, upon the way in which this is made available for the whole year, namely, by the construction of canals and ponds throughout the land, to which the water is conducted from the Nile by forcing machines, or by actually carrying it in vessels up to the fields and plantations.<note placement="foot">Upon the ancient monuments we find not only the draw-well with the long rope, which is now called <hi type="italic">Shaduf</hi>, depicted in various ways (see Wilkinson, i. p. 35, ii. 4); but at <hi type="italic">Beni-Hassan</hi> there is a representation of two men carrying a water-vessel upon a pole on their shoulders, which they fill from a draw-well or pond, and then carry to the field (cf. Hengstenberg, <hi type="italic">Egypt and the Books of Moses</hi>, pp. 220-1).</note> <div eID="gen2275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2276" type="x-p"/> The expression, “with thy foot,” probably refers to the large pumping wheels still in use there, which are worked by the feet, and over which a long endless rope passes with pails attached, for drawing up the water (cf. <hi type="italic">Niebuhr, Reise,</hi> i. 149), the identity of which with the ἕλιξ described by <hi type="italic">Philo</hi> as ὑδρηλὸν ὄργανον (<hi type="italic">de confus. ling. </hi>i. 410) cannot possibly be called in question; provided, that is to say, we do not confound this ἕλιξ with the Archimedean water-screw mentioned by <hi type="italic">Diod. Sic.</hi> i. 34, and described more minutely at v. 37, the construction of which was entirely different (see my Archaeology, ii. pp. 111-2). - The Egyptians, as genuine heathen, were so thoroughly conscious of this peculiar characteristic of their land, which made its fertility far more dependent upon the labour of human hands than upon the rain of heaven or divine providence, that <hi type="italic">Herodotus</hi> (ii. 13) represents them as saying, “The Greeks, with their dependence upon the gods, might be disappointed in their brightest hopes and suffer dreadfully from famine.” The land of Canaan yielded no support to such godless self-exaltation, for it was “a land of mountains and valleys, and drank water of the rain of heaven” (ל before מטר, to denote the external cause; see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §217, <hi type="italic">d</hi>.); i.e., it received its watering, the main condition of all fertility, from the rain, by the way of the rain, and therefore through the providential care of God. <div eID="gen2276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2277" type="x-p"/> It was a land which Jehovah inquired after, i.e., for which He cared (דּרשׁ, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.31.13">Pro 31:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.3.4">Job 3:4</reference>); His eyes were always directed towards it from the beginning of the year to the end; a land, therefore, which was dependent upon God, and in this dependence upon God peculiarly adapted to Israel, which was to live entirely to its God, and upon His grace alone. <div eID="gen2277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2278" type="x-p"/> This peculiarity in the land of Canaan led Moses to close the first part of his discourse on the law, his exhortation to fear and love the Lord, with a reference to the blessing that would follow the faithful fulfilment of the law, and a threat of the curse which would attend apostasy to idolatry.
entries.0c08767f3a8ff61e5a69ebe973dbd1bc4ef4dbec: <reference osisRef="Deut.11.13-Deut.11.15">Deu 11:13-15</reference> <div eID="gen2278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2279" type="x-p"/> If Israel would serve its God in love and faithfulness, He would give the land early and latter rain in its season, and therewith a plentiful supply of food for man and beast (see <reference osisRef="Lev.26.3">Lev 26:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.26.5">Lev 26:5</reference>; and for the further expansion of this blessing, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.1-Deut.28.12">Deu 28:1-12</reference>).
entries.41a6e34cbcd51ce99439dda260df8fc65f8872bf: <reference osisRef="Deut.11.16-Deut.11.25">Deu 11:16-25</reference> <div eID="gen2279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2280" type="x-p"/> But if, on the other hand, their heart was foolish to turn away from the Lord and serve other gods, the wrath of the Lord would burn against them, and God would shut up the heaven, that no rain should fall and the earth should yield no produce, and they would speedily perish (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.26.19-Lev.26.20">Lev 26:19-20</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deut.28.23-Deut.28.24">Deu 28:23-24</reference>). Let them therefore impress the words now set before them very deeply upon themselves and their children (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.18-Deut.11.21">Deu 11:18-21</reference>, in which there is in part a verbal repetition of <reference osisRef="Deut.6.6-Deut.6.9">Deu 6:6-9</reference>). The words, “<hi type="italic">as the days of the heaven above the earth</hi>,” i.e., as long as the heaven continues above the earth, - in other words, to all eternity (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.89.30">Psa 89:30</reference>; Job. <reference osisRef="Deut.14.12">Deu 14:12</reference>), - belong to the main sentence, “<hi type="italic">that your days may be multiplied</hi>,” etc. (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.21">Deu 11:21</reference>). “The promise to give the land to Israel for ever was not made unconditionally; an unconditional promise is precluded by the words, 'that your days may be multiplied'” (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>). (For further remarks, see at <reference osisRef="Deut.30.3">Deu 30:3</reference>-5.) For (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.22-Deut.11.25">Deu 11:22-25</reference>) if they adhered faithfully to the Lord, He would drive out before them all the nations that dwelt in the land, and would give them the land upon which they trod in all its length and breadth, and so fill the Canaanites with fear and terror before them, that no one should be able to stand against them. (On <reference osisRef="Deut.11.23">Deu 11:23</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.7.1-Deut.7.2">Deu 7:1-2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.1">Deu 9:1</reference>, and Deu 1:28.) The words, “every place whereon the soles of your feet shall tread shall be yours,” are defined more precisely, and restricted to the land of Canaan on both sides of the Jordan by the boundaries which follow: “<hi type="italic">from the desert</hi> (of Arabia on the south), <hi type="italic">and Lebanon</hi> (on the north), <hi type="italic">and from the river Euphrates</hi> (on the east) <hi type="italic">to the hinder sea</hi>” (the Mediterranean on the west; see Num 34:6). The Euphrates is given as the eastern boundary, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.1.7">Deu 1:7</reference>, according to the promise in Gen 15:18. (On <reference osisRef="Deut.11.25">Deu 11:25</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.7.24">Deu 7:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.2.25">Deu 2:25</reference>, and Exo 23:27.)
entries.16ac5e16eb996fa918b44fb61b59bf0c4fd26547: <reference osisRef="Deut.11.26-Deut.11.30">Deu 11:26-30</reference> <div eID="gen2280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2281" type="x-p"/> Concluding summary. “<hi type="italic">I set before you this day the blessing and the curse</hi>.” The blessing, if (אשׁר, ὅτε, as in <reference osisRef="Lev.4.22">Lev 4:22</reference>) ye hearken to the commandments of your God; the curse, if ye do not give heed to them, but turn aside from the way pointed out to you, to go after other gods. To this there are added instructions in <reference osisRef="Deut.11.29">Deu 11:29</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.11.30">Deu 11:30</reference>, that when they took possession of the land they should <hi type="italic">give</hi> the blessing upon Mount Gerizim and the curse upon Mount Ebal, i.e., should give utterance to them there, and as it were transfer them to the land to be apportioned to its inhabitants according to their attitude towards the Lord their God. (For further comment, see at Deu 27:14.) The two mountains mentioned were selected for this act, no doubt because they were opposite to one another, and stood, each about 2500 feet high, in the very centre of the land not only from west to east, but also from north to south. Ebal stands upon the north side, Gerizim upon the south; between the two is <hi type="italic">Sichem</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">Nabulus</hi>, in a tolerably elevated valley, fertile, attractive, and watered by many springs, which runs from the south-east to the north-west from the foot of Gerizim to that of Ebal, and is about 1600 feet in breadth. The blessing was to be uttered upon Gerizim, and the curse upon Ebal; though not, as the earlier commentators supposed, because the peculiarities of these mountains, viz., the fertility of Gerizim and the barrenness of Ebal, appeared to accord with this arrangement: for when seen from the valley between, “the sides of both these mountains are equally naked and sterile;” and “the only exception in favour of the former is a small ravine coming down, opposite the west end of the town, which is indeed full of foundations and trees” (<hi type="italic">Rob. Pal.</hi> iii. 96, 97). The reason for selecting Gerizim for the blessings was probably, as <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi> supposes, the fact that it was situated on the south, towards the region of the light. “Light and blessing are essentially one. From the light-giving face of God there come blessing and life (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.11">Psa 16:11</reference>).” - In <reference osisRef="Deut.11.30">Deu 11:30</reference> the situation of these mountains is more clearly defined: they were “<hi type="italic">on the other side of the Jordan</hi>,” i.e., in the land to the west of the Jordan, “<hi type="italic">behind the way of the sunset</hi>,” i.e., on the other side of the road of the west, which runs through the land on the west of the Jordan, just as another such road runs through the land on the east (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>). The reference is to the main road which ran from Upper Asia through Canaan to Egypt, as was shown by the journeys of Abraham and Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.6">Gen 12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.33.17-Gen.33.18">Gen 33:17-18</reference>). Even at the present day the main road leads from Beisan to Jerusalem round the east side of Ebal into the valley of Sichem, and then again eastwards from Gerizim through the Mukra valley on towards the south (cf. <hi type="italic">Rib</hi>. iii. 94; <hi type="italic">Ritter, Erdkunde,</hi> xvi. pp. 658-9). “<hi type="italic">In the land of the Canaanite who dwells in the Arabah</hi>.” By the <hi type="italic">Arabah</hi>, <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> understands the plain of <hi type="italic">Nabulus</hi>, which is not much less than four hours’ journey long, and on an average from a half to three-quarters broad, “the largest of all upon the elevated tract of land between the western plain and the valley of the Jordan” (<hi type="italic">Rob</hi>. iii. p. 101). This is decidedly wrong, however, as it is opposed to the fixed use of the word, and irreconcilable with the character of this plain, which, Robinson says, “is cultivated throughout and covered with the rich green of millet intermingled with the yellow of the ripe corn, which the country people were just reaping” (<hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> iii. 93). The <hi type="italic">Arabah</hi> is the western portion of the <hi type="italic">Ghor</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.1.1">Deu 1:1</reference>), and is mentioned here as that portion of the land on the west of the Jordan which lay stretched out before the eyes of the Israelites who were encamped in the steppes of Moab. “<hi type="italic">Over against Gilgal</hi>,” i.e., not the southern <hi type="italic">Gilgal</hi> between Jericho and the Jordan, which received its name for the first time in <reference osisRef="Josh.4.20">Jos 4:20</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.5.9">Jos 5:9</reference>; but probably the Gilgal mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.9.6">Jos 9:6</reference>; Jos 10:6., and very frequently in the history of Samuel, Elijah, and Elisha, which is only about twelve and a half miles from Gerizim in a southern direction, and has been preserved in the large village of <hi type="italic">Jiljilia</hi> to the south-west of Sinjil, and which stands in such an elevated position, “close to the western brow of the high mountain tract,” that you “have here a very extensive prospect over the great lower plain, and also over the sea, whilst the mountains of Gilead are seen in the east” (<hi type="italic">Rob</hi>. <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> iii. 81). Judging from this description of the situation, Mount Gerizim must be visible from this Gilgal, so that Gerizim and Ebal might very well be described as over against Gilgal.<note placement="foot">There is much less ground for the opinion of <hi type="italic">Winer</hi>, <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>, that Gilgal is the <hi type="italic">Jiljule</hi> mentioned by Robinson (<hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. iii. 47; and <hi type="italic">Bibl. Researches</hi>, p. 138), which evidently corresponds to the<hi type="italic">Galgula</hi> placed by <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> six Roman miles from<hi type="italic">Antipatris</hi>, and is situated to the south-east of <hi type="italic">Kefr Saba</hi> (<hi type="italic">Antipatris</hi>), on the road from Egypt to Damascus. For this place is not only farther from Gerizim and Ebal, viz., about seventeen miles, but from its position in the lowland by the sea-shore it presents no salient point for determining the situation of the mountains of Gerizim and Ebal. Still less can we agree with <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, who speaks of the village of<hi type="italic">Kilkilia</hi>, to the north-east of <hi type="italic">Kefr Saba</hi>, as the name itself has nothing in common with Gilgal.</note> <div eID="gen2281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2282" type="x-p"/> The last definition, “<hi type="italic">beside the terebinths of Moreh</hi>,” is intended no doubt to call to mind the consecration of that locality even from the times of the patriarchs (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>: see at <reference osisRef="Gen.12.6">Gen 12:6</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Gen.35.4">Gen 35:4</reference>).
entries.398349af35edc2f61c5ec925304ccff3d3c277e9: <reference osisRef="Deut.11.31-Deut.11.32">Deu 11:31-32</reference> <div eID="gen2282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2283" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Deut.11.31-Deut.11.32">Deu 11:31-32</reference> contain the reason for these instructions, founded upon the assurance that the Israelites were going over the Jordan and would take possession of the promised land, and should therefore take care to keep the commandments of the Lord (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.4.5-Deut.4.6">Deu 4:5-6</reference>). B. Exposition of the Principal Laws - Deuteronomy 12-26 <div eID="gen2283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2284" type="x-p"/> The statutes and rights which follow in the second or special half of this address, and which consist in part of rules having regard to circumstances not contemplated by the Sinaitic laws, and partly of repetitions of laws already given, were designed as a whole to regulate the ecclesiastical, civil, and domestic life of Israel in the land of Canaan, in harmony with its calling to be the holy nation of the Lord. Moses first of all describes the religious and ecclesiastical life of the nation, in its various relations to the Lord (ch. 12-16:17); and then the political organization of the congregation, or the rights and duties of the civil and spiritual leaders of the nation (Deut 16:18-18:22); and lastly, seeks to establish upon a permanent basis the civil and domestic well-being of the whole congregation and its individual members, by a multiplicity of precepts, intended to set before the people, as a conscientious obligation on their part, reverence and holy awe in relation to human life, to property, and to personal rights; a pious regard for the fundamental laws of the world; sanctification of domestic life and of the social bond; practical brotherly love towards the poor, the oppressed, and the needy; and righteousness of walk and conversation (ch. 19-26). - So far as the arrangement of this address is concerned, the first two series of these laws may be easily regarded as expositions, expansions, and completions of the commandments in the decalogue in relation to the Sabbath, and to the duty of honouring parents; and in the third series also there are unquestionably many allusions to the commandments in the second table of the decalogue. But the order in which the different laws and precepts in this last series are arranged, does not follow the order of the decalogue, so as to warrant us in looking there for the leading principle of the arrangement, as <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi> has done. Moses allows himself to be guided much more by analogies and the free association of ideas than by any strict regard to the decalogue; although, no doubt, the whole of the book of Deuteronomy may be described, as <hi type="italic">Luther</hi> says, as “a very copious and lucid explanation of the decalogue, an acquaintance with which will supply all that is requisite to a full understanding of the ten commandments.” <div eID="gen2284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2285" type="x-p"/> The laws relating to the worship of the Israelites commence with a command to destroy and annihilate all places and memorials of the Canaanitish worship (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.2-Deut.12.4">Deu 12:2-4</reference>), and then lay it down as an established rule, that the Israelites were to worship the Lord their God with sacrifices and gifts, only in the place which He Himself should choose (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.5-Deut.12.14">Deu 12:5-14</reference>). On the other hand, in the land of Canaan cattle might be slain for eating and the flesh itself be consumed in any place; though sacrificial meals could only be celebrated in the place of the sanctuary appointed by the Lord (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.15-Deut.12.19">Deu 12:15-19</reference>). Moreover, on the extension of the borders of the land, oxen, and sheep, and goats could be slaughtered for food in any place; but the blood was not to be eaten, and consecrated gifts and votive sacrifices were not to be prepared as meals anywhere, except at the altar of the Lord (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.20-Deut.12.28">Deu 12:20-28</reference>). Lastly, the Israelites were not to be drawn aside by the Canaanites, to imitate them in their worship (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.29-Deut.12.31">Deu 12:29-31</reference>).  <chapter eID="Deut.11"/> <div eID="gen2285" type="x-p"/>

entries.2fb84681e398d3c06879a525cc26c5436dfc60a1: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.11.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.11.1" sID="gen8726" type="section"/> <div sID="gen8727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">Therefore thou shalt love the Lord thy God.</hi> The whole address has this scope, that the people should testify their gratitude by their obedience, and thus being allured by God’s bounties, should reverently embrace His Law. On this account also, he requires them to love God, before he exhorts them to obey the Law itself. For, although he might have imperiously and menacingly commanded them, he preferred to lead them gently to obedience, by setting before them the sweetness of His grace. In sum, he exhorts them that, being invited by God’s love, they should love him in return. Meanwhile, it is well to observe that free affection is the foundation and beginning of duly obeying the Law, for what is drawn forth by constraint, or servile fear, cannot please God. He designates the precepts of the Law by various names, in order that they may zealously and attentively apply themselves to listen to God, who has omitted nothing calculated to regulate their life; for, by this variety of words, he signifies that God had familiarly and perfectly taught whatever was required. As to the three latter words, “his statutes, and judgments, and commandments,” what I have observed in Genesis and in the Psalms may be referred to. The word <foreign xml:lang="he">משמות</foreign>,<note n="254"> <div sID="gen8728" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="he">משמרת</foreign><hi type="italic">. A. V., charge. </hi>The LXX. keeps closest to the Hebrew idiom, <foreign xml:lang="el">φυλάξη τὰ φυλάγματα ἄυτου</foreign>. — W.<div eID="gen8728" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic">meshamroth, </hi>or guards, <hi type="italic">(custodiae,) </hi>which here stands first, is spoken in commendation of the Law on this ground, that it fences in our life, as it were, with rails, lest it should be exposed to errors on the right hand and on the left,. At the end of the verse he exhorts them to perseverance, because it was not allowable for the recollection<hi type="italic"> </hi>of their deliverance ever to cease.<div eID="gen8727" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.11.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen8726" osisID="Deut.11.1" type="section"/>
entries.09038afe685026c06105b70f3a903760431efa6d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.11.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.11.2" sID="gen8729" type="section"/> <div sID="gen8730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> <hi type="italic">And know ye this day.</hi> He again confirms the preceding sentence; because they had been more than sufficiently taught by the illustrious acts of God, how great was His power and how remarkable His mercy toward themselves. Two meanings may be given to the words; for some connect them thus, “Know ye this day the chastisement of the Lord,” and include in a parenthesis the clause, “for I speak not with your children, which have not known, and have not seen;” but others read the word of exhortation “know ye” separately, and<note n="255"> <div sID="gen8731" type="x-p"/> Tellement que tont le reste va son train. — <hi type="italic">Fr</hi>.<div eID="gen8731" type="x-p"/> </note> without any connection. The latter view pleases me best; although it little affects the substance of the matter which exposition we follow. For Moses admonishes them, that, if they only pay attention to the works of God, His glory, which may instruct them to fear Him, may be clearly beheld in them. In order, however, to urge them more vehemently, he adds, that he does not speak to posterity, to which the fame of these miracles would reach, but that he addresses eye-witnesses, who need no proof of them, having been assured of them by certain experience. He celebrates in many expressions of eulogy these miracles, whereby God had testified to them His power and goodness, lest they should lightly pass by what was worthy of their most earnest attention, and constant meditation. I forbear now to speak of other points, which I have elsewhere commented on. The word <foreign xml:lang="he">מוסר</foreign><note n="256"> <div sID="gen8732" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="he">מוסר</foreign> <hi type="italic">S.M.</hi> has rendered this word <hi type="italic">castigatio. V</hi>., disciplina. The root is <foreign xml:lang="he">יסר</foreign>; and both the root and noun meaning to correct and correction, will sometimes mean to chastise, etc. — <hi type="italic">W</hi><div eID="gen8732" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic"> musar, </hi>which stands first, is general, and extends to all the specific terms that follow; some, therefore, improperly render it “chastisement.” Where it is said at the end of verse 4, that the Egyptians were “destroyed unto that day,” we must understand that the effects of the slaughter, wherewith God destroyed them, were felt as if still present.<div eID="gen8730" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.11.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen8729" osisID="Deut.11.2" type="section"/>
